Organizations that want to take a targeted approach to their team and talent development often need a simple yet effective tool to assess the potential and performance of their employees. The 9-Box Grid Model has been a widely used tool for identifying and monitoring performance, talents, and potential for many years. In this article, you’ll learn how to use this tool and what key considerations to keep in mind when introducing it to your organization.

What is the 9-Box Model?

The “9-Box” is a relatively simple yet powerful tool for identifying, retaining, and developing talented employees. This can be done at both the individual and team levels. That’s why, in addition to talent development, it’s also valuable for team development or, for example, strategic workforce planning. The model maps out employees’ potential and talent and compares them to their performance. This makes it easier to identify high performers, “future leaders,” or potential successors for specific roles within a team. It also allows you to better identify which employees’ performance may still fall short of their potential and where there may still be opportunities for growth. [caption id="attachment_20147" align="aligncenter" width="500"] source: www.aihr.com[/caption]

Origins of the Model

The 9-Box Grid Model has been around for a long time. It was developed in the 1970s by the consulting firm McKinsey. It was initially used to compare business teams with one another. This allowed companies to better determine which business units required investment. Its use gained international recognition when the American company General Electric began applying it. The famous CEO Jack Welch placed strong emphasis on improving performance by attracting and retaining the right people. The model later evolved into a well-known HR tool for measuring the performance and potential of teams and individual employees.

Using the 9-Box Matrix

Today, the model remains the most widely used performance matrix internationally. As a result, many internationally oriented companies also use it. For users of the hrmforce development platform, the 9-Box Matrix is available as a standard feature. This makes it possible to gain a clear overview of the entire organization or specific units relatively quickly. This is achieved by having managers evaluate employees according to the model along two axes: their potential and their performance. This creates a grid of nine quadrants into which employees are categorized. For each organization and team, you can specify who is authorized to assign scores and who can view the results.

In this video, you’ll see how it works:

Using the Results

The results provide a quick overview of employees’ performance, talents, and potential. This is valuable for facilitating discussions among managers using a consistent framework. It helps ensure targeted investments in areas such as talent and team development. The results can also be used to foster constructive conversations between managers and employees, such as those focused on career development.

Benefits of the 9-Box Grid Model

The 9-box grid offers several advantages for organizations that use it, including compared to other available models. Organizations that use it often cite these benefits for monitoring and facilitating talent and team development:
  • The simple model powerfully simplifies the identification of high-potential employees or potential leaders.
  • It provides a standardized way to evaluate employees in their current roles. This makes it easier to assess performance and potential consistently and to compare employees.
  • Talent identification: The 9-Box helps organizations identify high-potential employees so they can offer them the right resources and opportunities for further development.
  • The model is transparent and provides employees with an honest view of how the organization assesses their potential.
  • The model provides a valuable overview of the existing employee population at a glance. This enables organizations to optimize their talent management and make sound decisions regarding employee development and career planning.
  • The model can help organizations set quality standards for employees and evaluate performance against these standards. This enables organizations to improve performance standards and encourage employees to reach their full potential.
  • Recruit fewer new employees. With a better understanding of the existing workforce and its potential, it becomes easier to retain key talent, reducing the need to recruit them. This can help prevent high-potential employees from leaving.
A well-known drawback is that the assessment can be quite subjective, especially when a single manager assigns the scores. In such cases, objective data-such as questionnaires for 360-degree feedback or the use of motivation tests or personality assessments for talent or team development-is not utilized. However, the subjective view resulting from a one-sided assessment can be broadened by involving multiple people in assigning scores to employees.

Points to Consider When Implementing the 9-Box Grid

To get the most out of the 9-Box Grid Model as an organization, effective implementation of the approach is essential in addition to the online tool. To this end, discuss internally with teams why and how the model is used, as well as the criteria that play a role in the assessment. These criteria typically relate to both performance and behavior. Also specify what follow-up steps are taken after an employee has been placed in a particular quadrant. It should not become a “judgmental model.” Define and clarify the different quadrants of the model as well. After all, how do you define “low,” “average,” or “high” performance internally? Where possible, align these definitions with internal job or competency profiles. Keep the model up to date by regularly assessing employees’ performance and potential. Continue to adapt the model over time to the organization’s changing needs. Once all employees have received a score, it’s time to discuss the results. Managers gain valuable insight into the composition of their team in terms of performance and potential. These results provide a solid foundation for strategically advancing the team’s development and growth. After all, what does the team want to achieve in the future? The 9-Box Model can also help answer this question and provide a roadmap for achieving that goal.

What do the 9 boxes mean?

The 9-Box classification model consists of nine boxes, each representing a specific combination of performance and potential. They’re almost self-explanatory, but at their core, they have the following meanings:
  • Box 1: Low Performance/Low Potential: These employees may not have the right skills or motivation to improve their performance and reach their potential. What does this mean for the future? Can the organization still help with their development?
  • Box 2: Average Performance/Low Potential: Employees perform at an average level but show little potential for growth and development. The organization can explore ways to motivate these employees and support their development.
  • Box 3: Low Performance/Average Potential: Performance is low, but there is potential for growth and development. The organization can help these employees develop, for example through training and coaching.
  • Box 4: High Performance/Low Potential: When high performance is combined with little potential for growth and development, the organization can reward employees for their performance. However, it should also explore new ways to motivate and challenge these employees.
  • Box 5: Average performance/Average potential: This group, which is quite average in terms of performance and potential, can be supported in their development by challenging them to reach their potential.
  • Box 6: Low Performance/High Potential: There’s still plenty of room for improvement here! An organization can help these employees develop and challenge them to reach their potential.
  • Box 7: High Performance/Average Potential: The organization can reward these employees for their performance and challenge them to further develop their potential.
  • Box 8: Average Performance/High Potential: Employees perform at an average level but show great potential for growth and development. The organization can support these employees’ development and challenge them to reach their potential.
  • Box 9: High Performance/High Potential: These employees are valuable assets to the organization! They should be encouraged and rewarded to reach their potential. The organization should also look for ways to involve them in the organization’s development.

Integrity in the workplace is an important and fundamental value for many organizations. So it makes sense that they would want to measure it. But measuring integrity can be quite challenging. As part of feedback for employees themselves, it’s not too difficult, but when it comes to broader personality assessments for recruitment and selection, things quickly become more complex. In this article, you’ll learn how to approach measuring integrity in an organization in a way that’s both valuable and responsible.

The Challenge of Measuring Integrity

Integrity is a personal trait that ensures you are honest, sincere, and consistent-and, for example, not susceptible to bribery. Employees who act honestly, reliably, and responsibly contribute to a stimulating and healthy work culture and to the achievement of business goals. Measuring integrity can therefore be valuable and insightful for organizations-including during the recruitment and selection process. After all, as an organization, you want to know what kind of people you’re bringing on board. Still, measuring integrity in the workplace is quite complex. Integrity tests can certainly be useful, but it’s important to look beyond just the numbers and test results. It also depends on the purpose of the assessment. As part of a feedback survey for employees themselves, it’s certainly a useful tool. However, when used as part of recruitment and selection processes, it becomes more complex. Why is that, exactly?

Scientific Research on Reliability

Over the past few decades, a great deal of scientific research has been conducted on the reliability of integrity assessments and the context in which these assessments take place. In these assessments-especially in recruitment and selection-the following factors often complicate matters:

  1. Social desirability

People want to present themselves in the best possible light, especially during job interviews. This can lead to socially desirable responses, causing candidates to portray themselves as more honest or ethical than their actual behavior suggests.

  1. Overestimation of One’s Own Behavior

Various studies show that people often unconsciously and sincerely overestimate their own behavior when it comes to ethics and integrity.

  1. Complexity of Behavior

Integrity is a broad concept and certainly not just black and white. What is seen as “ethical” behavior in one situation may be considered unethical in another. Moreover, it is not a fixed trait or a one-time achievement. It is something you can work on, and environmental or organizational influences (which, in turn, can change) play an important role in this process. Many studies emphasize that a high integrity score does not automatically mean that someone actually behaves with integrity. This is partly due to the risk of socially desirable responses, as this 1993 American study already demonstrated. However, reliability does appear to increase when questions focus on behavior in a specific context, as this study and other research have shown. For example, integrity surveys among students proved to be more reliable when questions focused on their behavior in a specific situation, such as “at school” or “at the university.”

How can you make effective use of integrity surveys?

For a broad integrity policy within an organization, it is valuable to make integrity a regular topic of discussion. Not only during recruitment and selection, but also, for example, at regular intervals within the standard review cycle. Take the context of behavior into account and invest in a culture of openness where employees feel involved in promoting ethical behavior. When it comes to providing employees with feedback on their self-awareness, performance, or development opportunities (such as 360-degree feedback), these assessments are definitely useful. For other personality assessments, we at hrmforce recommend exercising caution with these measurements. If you do wish to use them for recruitment and selection, you must be sure to thoroughly discuss and explain the results. Otherwise, it can become a sensitive issue that may be misinterpreted. An important point to consider is the difference between a person’s personality-which relates to aptitude and potential-and behavior that is actually observable. You cannot conclude, based on the measured results, whether someone is or is not a person of integrity. It does, however, say something about their potential for development. And keep the previously mentioned context in mind. If an integrity score comes out somewhat “lower,” you can also ask about specific past (work) situations during interviews. How did the person handle those situations? You can find more specific interview questions in the hrmforce competency handbook.

What else can your organization do to promote integrity?

In addition to making integrity a recurring topic of discussion and fostering an open culture, paying attention to the context of behavior is a key focus area. In addition to testing behavior or personality traits, you can therefore also develop tests (or conduct interviews) that focus on the specific context in which the behavior occurs. This can be done, for example, using scenarios in which candidates or participants describe how they would act in certain situations. Furthermore, organizations can invest in structured behavioral observation and, for example, feedback methods such as 360-degree feedback. This can certainly yield valuable information for the intended purpose.

Integrity and Organizing Leadership

In the field of leadership development, integrity is a key focus area-for example, when facilitating and developing organizational leadership. Among all the leadership styles that exist-and the many hybrid forms thereof-this one has been gaining significant traction in recent years. In addition to greater self-awareness across different levels of the organization, a clear Leadership Operating System (LOS) can also significantly increase and accelerate the impact of organizational leadership. It serves as a framework for discussions, shared protocols, and communication and decision-making flows that enable leaders to “steer” the organization in the right direction.

Anyone who has to choose a major at the start of or during their career faces a major challenge. After all, how do you know if a degree program is really the right fit for you? And how do you avoid making the wrong choice? This happens quite often. A good college major assessment test offers a solution and helps you make a better choice that aligns with your personality, intelligence, and motivations.

Why take a college major selection test?

Choosing a degree program is an exciting and important moment. For high school students, this usually happens during or at the end of high school. But even during their careers, people are increasingly choosing to pursue a degree to change direction or to seek further depth and specialization. Many employers facilitate this to encourage employee development or, for example, to enhance long-term employability . A college selection test helps with making a career choice or selecting a specific (advanced) degree program. This is by no means a luxury, as recent research shows that many people would like better guidance in making this decision. As many as 1 in 5 students feel they did not receive sufficient guidance in this regard. As a result, as many as one-quarter have at some point started a program of study without completing it. In practice, career guidance in schools often proves to be too limited. In higher professional education (HBO) and university education, the dropout rate is even higher (50.9 percent!), mainly due to choosing the wrong program. As a result, 31 percent drop out as early as the first year because the program does not meet their expectations, according to the Dutch Education Inspectorate. Students primarily indicate that their course selection could be improved through a college selection test and, for example, assistance from a professional college selection advisor or a conversation with someone who has just graduated.

Different Types of Tests

Anyone who wants to make a well-informed choice of study program that suits their personality, intelligence, and motivations can take a college selection test. These tests come in various forms. The free online tests are rather superficial, so you shouldn’t expect too much from them. If you want to take a well-structured test, you can easily take a good general career choice test for a small fee. At hrmforce, you also have the option to expand this assessment with a deeper focus on your personality, intelligence, and motivation. This can also include online feedback for additional explanation. This can be extremely valuable when making such a choice, especially since it can have a major impact on your life and career. What’s more, what makes hrmforce’s career choice test unique is that it-finally-objectively maps out all Dutch degree programs in this field. Not only are a participant’s interests assessed, but their answers are also compared to a normative group. This provides particularly valuable insights.

Benefits of College Choice Tests

Taking a well-researched college selection test offers several benefits. First and foremost, it helps you make a well-considered career choice or select a degree program or further education. This reduces the likelihood of dropping out or feeling dissatisfied with the choice you’ve made. The test can also help identify programs or careers that someone had not previously considered or was unaware of. Even in cases of doubt or uncertainty, it provides a better understanding of the requirements and potential future career demands. In addition to providing insight into academic programs and careers, a good college selection test also enhances self-awareness-for example, by clarifying one’s own interests, skills, and strengths. This helps in choosing a program of study or even developing a personal career plan. In this way, students are also better prepared for their future careers.

A Challenge for Academic Advisors

In addition to good career choice assessments, there is another important consideration that can help people make better educational choices. Research from Utrecht University and Leiden University shows that academic advisors can also play a greater role in this regard. This is especially true because, contrary to popular belief, a good choice of study program isn’t made in a single moment. It’s a process, but one that often lacks a clear endpoint, according to the researchers. Even after a study choice has been made, it can still change-and this can actually be very helpful. However, there needs to be room for that flexibility, which is often lacking. The researchers therefore recommend that academic advisors continue to guide high school seniors, even after they’ve already chosen a program. They observed that people sometimes become fixated on a degree choice they’ve made for themselves. In doing so, they tend to ignore conflicting information. For example, if it turns out that the “chosen” degree program doesn’t actually align well with an interest that’s important to them. As a result, people sometimes close themselves off from the realization that a different program might be a better fit for them. It also appears that high school students, in particular, sometimes cling to a “choice” because people close to them (such as parents) believe that the earlier choice suits them better. In addition to providing longer-term, process-oriented guidance, the researchers suggest that academic advisors should also be aware that a student may be clinging to a study choice for the wrong reasons-even against their better judgment. Study advisors should therefore continue to reflect, together with prospective students, on a person’s interests and the programs that align with them. It should also be made clearer that it is not “strange” to change one’s choice of study program. By drawing attention to this, there is a growing awareness that changing one’s choice of study program can also lead to a better choice and better outcomes.

Tip: Forget about the “perfect” choice of study program

Finally, here’s a tip for anyone facing this decision themselves. First and foremost, back up your choice of major with reasons. A decision is made based on feelings, reason, and intuition. A good college major selection test can help with this. To also support the rational side of the decision, it helps to substantiate and justify your choice with arguments. These questions can help:
  • How do I know this program is right for me?
  • Why am I choosing this program? Or why am I considering it?
Here’s another important insight to consider. Prepare thoroughly for your college major decision-a college major assessment and a college advisor can be very helpful in this process. But don’t strive for the “perfect” choice either. After all, a program that perfectly matches who you are and what you want probably doesn’t exist. Many degree programs include courses, theory, or projects that aren’t a great fit for you. This doesn’t necessarily mean the program isn’t right for you. So focus on finding a program that’s “good enough” for you, according to a strategy from Studiekeuzemaken.nl. “Because if you strive for perfection, your doubts will never end.”

Initiate a dialogue and a process of change

DISC shows how people communicate, make decisions, and collaborate. But DISC’s greatest strength doesn’t lie in any one person-it emerges when different DISC colors complement each other.  In this article, you’ll discover which DISC colors work well together, where tension arises, and how to make the most of those differences. Want to brush up on what the DISC colors mean first? Then check out this article:

Similar DISC Colors: Easy Collaboration with Clear Pitfalls

When your behavior resembles that of your collaboration partner, pitfalls can arise.

Red and Red

Two Red styles work quickly and purposefully. They value clarity, pace, and direct communication. In time-sensitive situations, this is a powerful combination. The pitfall: a power struggle. Both want to lead, which can lead to conflicts. There may also be insufficient attention to consensus and details.

Yellow and yellow

Yellow and yellow bring energy, creativity, and optimism. Together, they generate countless ideas and create a lively atmosphere within a team. The pitfall: lack of follow-through. New ideas keep pouring in while ongoing projects are left unfinished.

Green and green

Two green styles form a harmonious and secure partnership. They listen, support one another, and show loyalty. The pitfall: conflicts are avoided. Decisions take a long time, and change moves slowly.

Blue and Blue

Blue and blue deliver quality, structure, and careful analysis. Mistakes are rarely made. The pitfall: “analysis paralysis.” Decisions can be delayed too long due to a drive for perfection.

Strong DISC Combinations: Different Styles That Complement Each Other

In a good team, people with different personality types complement each other.

Red and Green

Red brings direction and pace, while green ensures support and attention to people. This makes the combination very strong for change initiatives. The tension: Red wants to move faster than green is comfortable with, while green wants more coordination than red has patience for. Balance is achieved through mutual understanding.

Red and Blue

Red makes decisions; blue monitors quality and risks. Together, they ensure results that are both swift and well-thought-out. The tension: Blue sometimes finds Red too impulsive; Red finds Blue too slow.

Yellow and Blue

Yellow brings ideas and inspiration; blue makes plans concrete and achievable. This combination is perfect for concept development and innovation. The tension: Yellow feels held back by critical questions; blue gets frustrated by a constant stream of new ideas.

Yellow and Green

Yellow provides energy and momentum, while green fosters calm and collaboration. Teams feel both heard and inspired. The tension: Yellow sometimes moves too fast, while green often finds change too abrupt.

Red and Yellow

This combination excels in communication, sales, and entrepreneurship. Red provides direction; yellow brings influence and enthusiasm. The tension: both sometimes lack structure and attention to detail.

Green and Blue

Green focuses on people, blue on processes. Together, they create a reliable, stable way of working with clear agreements. The tension: blue can sometimes sound too critical, green too cautious.

DISC opposites: where friction arises

Red versus green

Red is direct and task-oriented; green is indirect and people-oriented. Without insight, they can irritate each other, but with understanding, they complement each other perfectly. Red helps make decisions; green ensures others follow through.

Yellow versus blue

Yellow thinks out loud, connects people, and improvises. Blue analyzes, plans, and monitors. Without insight, they clash quickly, but together they deliver creative and realistic solutions.

Which DISC colors best suit certain goals?

Note: The information below is a guideline and does not always apply.

For innovation and new ideas

Yellow for creativity, blue for feasibility, green for buy-in.

For rapid change

Red for direction, blue for quality, green for communication.

For stability and customer focus

Green for collaboration, blue for structure.

For complex projects

Blue for analysis and planning, red for decision-making, green for team cohesion.

How do you get the most out of DISC color differences?

1. Map out team members’ DISC profiles When people understand each other’s styles, mutual respect and better communication develop. 2. Use DISC as a language, not a label Don’t say: “You’re too critical.” Say: “You’re showing a lot of blue right now-can you explain the risks?” 3. Assign roles based on strengths Red for deadlines, yellow for communication, green for support, blue for planning. 4. Consciously balance teams Teams with only red and yellow lack structure. Teams with only green and blue lack momentum. 5. View tension as a useful signal Where there’s friction, there’s often exactly the quality you yourself lack. Differences aren’t a problem-they’re an opportunity. Find out here how to read a DISC report .

Finally: Which DISC colors work best together?

There is no such thing as a perfect combination of DISC colors. It’s not about “right” or “wrong,” but about balance. Similar colors create comfort but are one-sided. Different colors create tension but deliver strength, innovation, and better decisions. Take the DISC test here

Talent determines whether organizations grow or stagnate, yet many HR teams still rely on disparate tools, Excel spreadsheets, and subjective evaluations. Talent management system software brings coherence to talent processes and helps organizations make more informed decisions about their people, ensuring that performance, development, and career advancement are no longer evaluated in isolation from one another.

In short

  • Talent management system software helps organizations make well-informed decisions about employees.
  • A TMS brings performance, skills, development, and succession planning together in a single system.
  • Skills-based talent management only works when skills are clearly defined and used in a measurable way.
  • Without metrics, a TMS remains primarily a record-keeping system.
  • Manager adoption and data quality determine the outcome.

What is talent management system software?

Talent management system software, often abbreviated as TMS, is software that helps organizations track, develop, and deploy talent in a structured way. The system supports processes related to performance, skills, development, career advancement, and succession planning, ensuring that decisions about employees are made more consistently. A TMS is not a standalone HR application, but a platform that brings together multiple HR processes. By connecting these processes, it creates a single overview of talent within the organization, preventing information from becoming scattered across different systems.

Talent Management in Simple Terms

Talent management revolves around three interrelated questions: who demonstrates desired behavior and performance, who has room to grow further, and who can eventually take on a different or more demanding role. A TMS helps answer these questions by capturing data and combining it in a consistent manner.

What Does a Talent Management System Include?

Not every organization uses all components of a TMS at the same time, but the interconnection between components ensures that information from one process is used in another. Development agreements align with performance, and succession planning decisions are based on recorded data rather than isolated impressions.

Common components of TMS software

A talent management system typically includes modules for performance management-where goals and reviews are documented-as well as components for competencies and skills, which provide insight into what employees are capable of. In addition, many systems support learning and development to align professional growth with identified needs. Succession planning is also a common feature, as is support for internal promotion, feedback, and reports that provide an overview of trends and patterns.

Difference Between TMS, HRIS, and Performance Tools

The terms HRIS, performance tools, and TMS are often used interchangeably, even though they serve different purposes. An HRIS focuses primarily on personnel administration, such as data, contracts, and leave. Performance tools support discussions and goal-setting between employees and managers. A TMS combines information from these processes and supports decisions regarding development, career advancement, and succession planning.

Why Organizations Choose TMS Software

Organizations choose a TMS when standalone systems fail to provide sufficient visibility and talent processes become fragmented. Without cohesion, it is difficult to link performance, development, and succession planning, which often results in decisions being based on limited information.

Common Challenges

Without a TMS, there is often no up-to-date overview of skills, performance evaluations vary by manager, and succession planning is only discussed when an employee is about to leave. Additionally, training programs do not always align with performance, and information is scattered across multiple systems, making it difficult to identify patterns.

Skills-based talent management: More than just a trend

Skills-based talent management focuses on what employees can do, rather than just on job titles. This helps organizations adapt more flexibly to change and better support internal mobility.

What Makes Skills Useful in Practice

Skills only become useful when they are clearly defined and used consistently. Without clear definitions, you end up with a list that offers little guidance. A workable approach starts with a limited number of core skills per job family, which are linked to observable behaviors and used in performance reviews and development.

Performance Management in Modern TMS Software

More and more organizations are moving away from annual reviews and opting for shorter cycles with regular discussions. A TMS supports this way of working by providing structure for goals, agreements, and documentation, without taking over the conversation between manager and employee.

The basic principle of performance management

The system supports the conversation and assists with documentation, but it does not replace the conversation nor does it determine its content.

Succession planning and insight into potential

Succession planning is all about continuity and preventing unexpected vacancies in roles. Organizations want to know who can take over a role, both in the short and long term, so that risks remain manageable.

How succession planning works in a TMS

Within a TMS, positions are designated as critical, and the employees identified as potential successors are documented. By combining performance, skills, and other data, a more well-founded assessment is created than when decisions are based solely on experience or visibility.

Why Assessments and Feedback Are Used

Without metrics, talent management remains primarily a way to record information. Metrics help better substantiate decisions and provide greater insight into differences among employees.

Examples of talent information used

Organizations often use personality questionnaires to gain insight into behavioral preferences, tests that reveal learning ability, and feedback tools that examine behavior from multiple perspectives. Combining this information provides a broader picture than relying on a single source.

Implementation: Where Things Often Go Wrong

When implementing a TMS, technology rarely proves to be the biggest obstacle. Adoption by managers and the quality of the data recorded determine whether the system is actually used. When definitions are unclear or processes are designed to be too complex, usage declines and the system loses its purpose within the organization.

Factors That Support Implementation

Clear agreements on terminology, a design that aligns with managers’ work, and clear rules regarding data usage ensure that a TMS is used and maintained more effectively.

KPIs for tracking talent management

Using metrics provides insight into whether talent management contributes to the organization’s goals. Commonly used indicators include internal promotion, succession planning, time to readiness, and retention of employees in key roles.

When should you choose a talent management suite?

A TMS is suitable for organizations that want to systematically support talent decisions and consolidate processes related to development and succession planning. If HR operates primarily on an operational basis and processes are not yet established, it may be wiser to start with simpler tools first.

FAQ

How much does talent management system software cost?

Costs vary by vendor and the system’s configuration. A monthly fee per employee is often charged, supplemented by setup and implementation support costs.

How long does implementation take?

An implementation usually takes a few months, depending on the size of the organization and the selected features.

Is a TMS suitable for smaller organizations?

Smaller organizations can also use a TMS, provided the scope remains limited and the system aligns with existing workflows.

In conclusion

Team performance is becoming increasingly crucial. But how do you ensure that those teams actually perform well? Team development allows you to work on this in a targeted way. It starts with analyzing team performance and the personalities within the team. By taking different team styles into account, everyone can then work on specific action items.  

The Rise of Team Development

Team development has been an important topic for organizations, their teams, and HR professionals for years. In recent years, this topic has rapidly risen on organizations’ priority lists. It has now even become the most important topic, according to an international study on HRM trends conducted by Deloitte in 130 countries, including the Netherlands. This is due to various developments, such as globalization, increasing economic dynamism, and customers (and other stakeholders) who have ever-higher expectations. As a result, collaboration in general has become increasingly important for the success of companies. This applies to collaboration between organizations as well as within organizations. We also see this reflected in the rapid rise of self-managing teams, project teams, “Scrum and Agile” work methods, and the emergence of virtual teams. New technology (online collaboration) naturally plays a key facilitating role in this development.  

It doesn’t happen on its own

Within organizations, a shift is underway from the old hierarchical management models toward more (multifunctional) team-based models. This leads to better performance and is a more effective model for operating successfully in today’s dynamic, less predictable business environment. In that environment, a successful team delivers the desired results; it is more effective and achieves better performance than the mere sum of the contributions made by individual team members. There is, however, a challenge. Effective teams usually do not emerge on their own. Team development is essential for helping a team perform better and excel. Otherwise, it remains simply a group of individuals. It’s striking that fewer than 20 percent of teams consider themselves “high-performing.” That means about 80 percent do not (yet)!  

Analyzing and Improving Team Performance

Most teams can work much more effectively than they often do. And often, even small interventions can lead to significant progress. “Team development” is the key term here. In this context, team training and leadership training have proven to be important (evidence-based) interventions. But at its core, the solution largely lies in how team performance and individual characteristics are analyzed, and in giving the team responsibility for improving its own performance. Paying attention to different team styles and the roles within teams is of great importance in this regard. At hrmforce, we’ve tailored the tools organizations use for their team development analyses to address this. Quite recently, we’ve even added additional components to highlight different team styles. After all, no two teams are alike, and the same applies to the environmental factors they face at different times.  

Different Teams and Environmental Factors

Of course, there are also many theories and conceptual models regarding the most effective composition of teams. Depending on the type of team, its objectives, and environmental factors, these theories and insights can be valuable for your team development. After all, do you want to ensure the success of complex projects? Then, as this research on multinational companies shows, you should ideally assemble a large team of highly educated specialists. The downside, however, is that highly educated specialists are often less willing to learn from one another, to share information (pro)actively, and to help each other distribute the work as effectively as possible. These can be important considerations for such a team, especially if the analysis of personal and team characteristics also points in that direction. Or is this an innovation team? In that case, performance pressure can be a key concern. Research by TNO shows that innovation teams actually become risk-averse under pressure, which makes innovations more likely to fail. Their advice: create a supportive work environment in which resilient innovative behavior can flourish. HRD experts can help the team in this regard and reduce their chances of failure, according to TNO.

Balance and Phases of Team Development

Another key consideration is the relationship between individual and team performance. Through effective collaboration, team members get more out of themselves and bring out the best in one another. Within teams, you naturally have to deal with individuals who strive to get the most out of their own careers. That is perfectly healthy in itself, but the balance must also remain healthy. As soon as individual ambitions come at the expense of the team, group dynamics can actually start to backfire. Team development can address this as well, naturally within the various stages of team development, as we described earlier.  

The Role of Managers

And then, of course, there is the important role of managers. Scientific research on team performance based on “serious gaming” using an escape room (by Friesland Boeit) also provided valuable new insights. This study examined team performance at the competency level, with a strong focus on leadership. “In today’s rapidly changing world and economy, leadership and collaboration are currently crucial areas of focus,” says leadership expert Jelle Dijkstra (lecturer in Personal Leadership & Innovation at NHL University of Applied Sciences), who was involved in the study. “But those are often the weak points right now. Organizations are saying they’ll ‘work differently’ and ‘collaborate differently,’ but how exactly? That question often remains unanswered.” A notable finding from years of research in the escape room is that the most successful teams have two leaders: a dominant leader and a social leader, who can take turns. They must be able to switch flexibly between different leadership styles, depending on their team, the environment, and their assignment.  

Action Items Following the Analysis

Teams are constantly evolving. That’s why regular analysis remains valuable. And after an analysis, concrete action items are, of course, necessary. With hrmforce’s specialized questionnaires focused on teams, it’s possible to map out team development (strengths and weaknesses). Based on talent and personal characteristics, tasks and goals can then be formulated for a development plan and an action plan. The renowned Big Five personality theory (centered on the five major dimensions: extraversion, agreeableness, emotional stability, conscientiousness, and openness) is valuable for conducting analyses and determining action items for team development. Our analyses are based on this theory.

Many organizations base their hiring decisions on resumes and experience, even though the real difference often lies in thinking skills. The Matrigma test provides insight into abstract reasoning ability, a key predictor of success in many roles. In this article, you’ll discover what Matrigma measures, what it doesn’t, and how to use the test effectively as part of a broader assessment approach.

In short

  • Matrigma measures abstract reasoning ability through nonverbal patterns and figure sequences.
  • The test is culture-neutral and suitable for international recruitment.
  • Matrigma does not measure language skills, numerical reasoning, motivation, or work behavior.
  • The test works best in combination with broader aptitude tests.
  • For job suitability, combining it with other assessments is often necessary.

What is the Matrigma test, and what exactly does it measure?

The Matrigma test is a nonverbal aptitude test that focuses on abstract logical thinking. Candidates are shown sequences of figures and must select the pattern that logically follows. No language is involved, and mathematical skills do not play a role. This test measures:
  • Pattern recognition
  • Logical reasoning
  • Problem-solving ability when faced with new challenges
This type of thinking is particularly important in roles where someone must quickly structure new information. Think of analytical, technical, or strategic roles. Important to know: Matrigma measures a single cognitive domain. Therefore, it does not provide a complete picture of a person’s intellectual abilities. Below is a sample question from a Matrigma test (source: Hellotest).

Is Matrigma an intelligence test or an aptitude test?

In an HR context, Matrigma is often referred to as an intelligence test. From a psychological perspective, it is more accurate to describe it as an aptitude test that measures a component of general intelligence. Matrigma focuses on abstract reasoning ability. This ability is related to the g-factor but does not represent all cognitive skills. Verbal interpretation, numerical insight, and practical reasoning ability are not assessed. Therefore, do not use Matrigma as the sole measure of intelligence. View it as a narrowly defined measurement tool within a broader context.

When should you use the Matrigma test in recruitment?

Matrigma works particularly well for roles with high cognitive complexity. For example, when someone:
  • Must solve new problems without relying on set procedures
  • Must quickly recognize patterns in unstructured information
  • Must switch between abstract concepts
Examples of suitable contexts:
  • Traineeships
  • Analytical roles
  • IT and data-related roles
  • Management roles involving strategic issues
For operational or highly routine positions, Matrigma often provides less relevant information. Source: Jobtestprep

When is Matrigma insufficient as the sole assessment tool?

Many HR teams make the mistake of using Matrigma as a standalone selection tool. This increases the risk of a one-sided assessment. Matrigma does not assess:
  • Language comprehension and written communication
  • Mathematical reasoning
  • Work style and behavior
  • Motivation and drivers
A candidate can score high on Matrigma and still struggle with reports, numbers, or collaboration. The reverse is also true. A lower score does not mean someone is less intelligent, but rather that their ability to think abstractly under time pressure is less developed. Source: Hellotest

How does Matrigma compare to other aptitude tests?

The main difference lies in the breadth of what is measured. Matrigma:
  • Measures only abstract reasoning ability
  • Is entirely nonverbal
  • Focuses on a single cognitive domain
Broader aptitude tests:
  • Also measure verbal and numerical reasoning
  • Provide a more complete picture of cognitive aptitude
  • Are better aligned with practical job requirements
One example of this is Hrmforce’s Ability Scan. This test combines multiple cognitive components into a single assessment. This gives you insight into various thinking skills that collectively predict job performance.

How do you interpret a low or high Matrigma score?

Matrigma scores always require context. A high score indicates a strong aptitude for abstract problem-solving. This is valuable for complex roles, but says nothing about motivation or practical application. A lower score often means:
  • Less preference for abstract puzzles
  • A greater need for concrete frameworks
  • Stronger performance in practical tasks
Important: Never use scores in isolation from job requirements and other data. Combine them with interviews, resume information, and additional assessments.

How do you combine Matrigma with other assessments?

The strength lies in combining assessments. Linking Matrigma to other tools creates a more complete profile. Common combinations:
  • Matrigma + broader aptitude test
  • Matrigma + personality assessment
  • Matrigma + motivation test
At Hrmforce, Matrigma-style information is often combined with the Ability Scan. This test measures verbal, numerical, and spatial reasoning. As a result, you can see not only whether someone can think abstractly, but also how that translates to daily work tasks.

What about validity and predictive value?

Research shows that cognitive ability tests have strong predictive value for job performance. This also applies to tests that measure abstract reasoning ability. The predictive value increases when:
  • The test aligns with the complexity of the job
  • You measure multiple cognitive domains
  • The results are combined with behavioral data
Matrigma performs particularly well in this regard for roles where abstract thinking plays a major part in the work. For broader roles, additional assessment is needed. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Me4vj_l6oeI

What does Matrigma mean for the candidate experience?

Candidates often find Matrigma challenging and fair, as language and prior knowledge have little influence. At the same time, the test raises questions, especially in the event of a rejection. Transparency is therefore important. Explain in advance:
  • What the test measures
  • Why you’re using it
  • How the results are used
This increases acceptance and understanding, even in the event of a less favorable outcome.

Frequently Asked Questions About the Matrigma Test

What does the Matrigma test measure? The test measures abstract reasoning ability through nonverbal figure sequences and patterns. Is Matrigma suitable for every position? No. The test is particularly suited for roles with high cognitive complexity and few routine tasks. Does the Matrigma test also measure numerical or verbal reasoning? No. Language and math skills are not part of the test. Can you use the Matrigma test as the sole selection tool? This is not recommended. The test measures a single cognitive aspect and lacks information on behavior and motivation. How long does the Matrigma test take? On average, about 40 minutes, depending on the version and the administration protocol. What does a low score indicate? A lower score often indicates a lower preference for abstract problem-solving, not low intelligence. How can you increase its predictive value? By combining Matrigma with broader aptitude tests and behavioral assessments.

How to Use Matrigma Effectively

If you want to use Matrigma effectively in your selection process, follow these steps:
  1. First, determine whether abstract thinking is truly relevant to the position.
  2. Never use Matrigma as the sole decision-making tool.
  3. Combine the results with a broader aptitude test.
  4. Include personality and motivation in your assessment.
  5. Clearly explain to candidates how you use the test.
This way, you’ll ensure that Matrigma isn’t just a standalone puzzle, but a valuable component of data-driven HR decision-making. see the Ability Scan to administer a cognitive aptitude test right away.

Many HR professionals are familiar with this scenario: a candidate makes a strong impression during the interview but performs differently than expected after being hired. An assessment during the hiring process helps you gain insight into a candidate’s potential, behavior, and capacity for development before hiring, so your selection is based on data rather than gut feeling.

In short

  • A pre-hire assessment predicts job performance better than an interview alone
  • The combination of ability, personality, and motivation provides the most reliable picture
  • Assessments measure potential, not just experience
  • Objective selection reduces mismatches and early turnover
  • Proper use requires interpretation and discussion, not just scores

 

What is a pre-employment assessment?

A job application assessment is a structured evaluation of traits that, taken together, indicate a candidate’s likelihood of success in a role. It’s not about what someone has done, but about what they are likely to demonstrate in terms of behavior, performance, and development. At its core, an assessment measures three dimensions:
  • cognitive ability
  • personality traits
  • motivation and drivers
Together, these layers form the foundation of workplace behavior. A resume describes the past. An assessment looks to the future. If you’d like to see how this works in practice, check out the page on online assessments .

Why is an assessment more reliable than a job interview?

Interviews are prone to bias. Sympathy, self-confidence, and communication style strongly influence judgment-often unconsciously. An assessment:
  • objectively compares candidates
  • looks beyond background or networks
  • highlights patterns in thinking and behavior
This results in a more realistic prediction of how a candidate will perform in practice.

What types of assessments are used in the hiring process?

Various types of assessments are conducted.

What does an aptitude test measure during a job application?

An aptitude test measures the ability to process new information, make connections, and solve problems. This ability determines how quickly someone learns and how they tackle complex tasks. Especially for positions with:
  • changing responsibilities
  • analytical challenges
  • independent decision-making
cognitive ability is a strong predictor of success. Important to know: It’s not about knowledge, but about thinking skills. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Xby8NLaqJEE

What does a personality assessment measure?

A personality assessment identifies behavioral tendencies. It shows how someone tends to act under normal circumstances and under pressure. Examples of what it reveals:
  • how someone collaborates
  • how someone handles responsibility
  • how someone responds to change
  • how someone makes decisions
The assessment does not judge right or wrong. It shows what likely comes naturally and what requires effort. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lc7vN_e36Yc&t=7s

What does a motivation questionnaire measure?

Motivation determines why someone wants to exhibit certain behaviors. Two people with the same profile may perform differently due to differences in their motivations. A motivation questionnaire provides insight into:
  • what gives someone energy
  • when someone stays engaged
  • what demotivates someone
This helps predict whether someone is likely to commit to a role or organization over the long term. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tf8VEEDfruY

When should you use an assessment during the hiring process?

The right timing determines the value of the tool. In practice, there are three logical points:

1. After an initial screening

You use the assessment to objectively compare several suitable candidates.

2. Before the in-depth interview

The results provide input for targeted questions. You test assumptions rather than making them.

3. When you’re torn between candidates

The assessment helps reveal differences that don’t come to light during interviews. Important: Never use an assessment on its own. Its strength lies in combining it with the interview.

What does an assessment reveal-and what doesn’t it reveal?

An assessment tells you a lot, but not everything.

What an assessment does

  • provide insight into potential
  • highlight development potential
  • identify risks

What an assessment does not do

  • guarantee behavior
  • replace experience
  • Take the full context into account
That is why the conversation remains essential. The assessment guides the conversation, not the other way around.

How do you prevent misinterpretation of assessment results?

A common mistake is reading scores literally. This leads to hasty conclusions and unjustified rejections. Proper interpretation requires:
  • an understanding of norm groups
  • insight into the relationships between factors
  • a conversation with the candidate
A score is not a judgment. It is a hypothesis that you test through dialogue. For example, a lower score on a competency does not mean that someone is unable to demonstrate that behavior. It says something about how naturally that behavior comes to them.

How does an assessment contribute to objective selection?

Objective selection means evaluating candidates based on job-relevant criteria, not on personal preference. An assessment supports this by:
  • standardized measurement tools
  • equal starting points for every candidate
  • transparent decision-making
This reduces the risk of unconscious bias and strengthens the rationale behind decisions communicated to management and the candidate.

What does this mean for turnover and performance?

Mismatch is one of the main causes of early departure. Often, this mismatch arises not from a lack of ability, but from differences in expectations, work style, or motivation. By making more accurate predictions in advance:
  • the likelihood of a sustainable placement increases
  • the quality of onboarding improves
  • the risk of attrition within the first year decreases
Assessment data helps you not only select candidates but also provide targeted guidance after they start.

How do assessments fit within legal and privacy regulations?

Clear rules apply in the Netherlands. Key principles:
  • only assess what is job-relevant
  • Be transparent with the candidate
  • Do not retain data longer than necessary
Candidates must know:
  • why they are taking an assessment
  • what happens to the results
  • who has access to the results
Proper use strengthens trust in the selection process.

Frequently Asked Questions About Job Application Assessments

What exactly does a job application assessment measure? It measures potential based on ability, personality, and motivation-not just experience. How reliable are online assessments? When properly standardized and interpreted, they have high predictive value. Can you reject someone based on an assessment? Yes, provided the assessment is job-relevant and forms part of a broader decision. How long does an assessment take on average? That varies depending on the assessment’s structure. Often between 30 and 75 minutes. What if a candidate doesn’t recognize themselves in the results? Then that serves as a topic for discussion. The dialogue is part of the interpretation. Are assessments also suitable for rare profiles? Especially then. They help identify potential that isn’t evident on the resume. Can you share assessment results with the candidate? Yes. Many organizations do this during or after the interview.

In conclusion: How to Use Assessments Effectively

If you want to use assessments effectively in the hiring process, follow these steps:
  1. Determine in advance what success in the role means
  2. Choose tools that align with that
  3. Combine the results with a structured interview
  4. Use scores as a starting point for dialogue
  5. Incorporate assessment data even after the candidate starts work
This way, an assessment becomes not just a selection tool in and of itself, but a resource for better decisions and sustainable growth. If you want to quickly see which tools are right for your situation, check out the assessment overview.

Getting the right person in the right place. For many recruiters, this is a challenge-but often a difficult one as well. It sometimes feels like looking for a needle in a haystack. Moreover, the entire hiring process can cause a great deal of stress when the right candidate needs to be found in a short amount of time. 9 tips for recruitment.

1. Develop a clear strategy

To get the right person in the right place, it’s wise to establish a strategy in advance. What qualifications should the ideal candidate have? Are you looking for a “junior” or “senior” employee? Should the candidate possess very specific knowledge, or be more versatile? How strict are the requirements? It’s worth taking the time to thoroughly analyze the role for each job opening and translate that into specific job requirements. Do you need to fill multiple positions? If so, rank them from highest to lowest priority.

2. Create a timeline

Is there a strict deadline for filling the position? Is a new project about to start for which the new employee is absolutely essential? If so, a timeline is crucial to ensure that the right candidate is found and hired on time. Such a timeline can be created based on existing data and allows for meticulous planning. How long did it take in the past for similar candidates to be hired?

3. Collaborate with other teams

By collaborating with the teams that will be working with the new colleague, you’ll significantly increase the chances of finding the right match. When a significant portion of communication takes place online, it’s important that everyone involved has access to a robust ATS (Applicant Tracking System) that allows you to effectively manage the recruitment process.

4. Take advantage of the benefits of an ATS

With the help of an Applicant Tracking System (ATS), recruiters can keep a close eye on exactly which positions each candidate has applied for, what stage of the application process they’re in, and what the findings are so far. Such a tracking system offers numerous possibilities for streamlining the application process down to the last detail.

5. Make it easy to apply

The easier it is for candidates to apply, the more people will do so. Also, make sure applicants can apply via computer, tablet, or smartphone. Send all candidates a notification when their application is received and explain the next steps in the process.

6. Ask the same questions during interviews

Give all candidates equal opportunities-that is, ask the same questions in the same order and ensure that the same colleagues are always involved in the interview.

7. Be consistent

Consistency is the key to an effective recruitment process. This means evaluating every candidate in the same way. That way, you can easily compare candidates and determine who is the best fit for the organization.

8. Collect data

To make the right decision, it can be extremely helpful to have gathered all kinds of data from previous recruitment processes. This allows you to avoid problems that occurred in the past and work more effectively.

9. Avoid biases

Bias has no place in the hiring process. This applies to every step of the application process. Bias can be prevented by involving multiple people from diverse backgrounds in the interviews. Additionally, rely on the facts and don’t let your personal feelings influence your judgment.

The DISC colors—red, yellow, green, and blue-provide a useful model for identifying behavioral and communication preferences. Rather than pigeonholing people, DISC shows which color or combination of colors matches your “nature.” This is helpful for personal development and teamwork.

A Brief Explanation of the DISC Colors

Imagine this: you want to make quick decisions and take action (lots of red), while your colleague wants to get everyone on board first and seek harmony (lots of green).

Without an understanding of DISC colors, this can sometimes lead to frustration. Using the language of colors, you’ll see that you both contribute something valuable and learn to understand each other better.

- Red: Dominant & decisive (D) - Yellow: Influential & inspiring (I) - Green: Stable & supportive (S) - Blue: Conscientious & analytical (C)

What You’ll Learn in This Article

  • Exactly what DISC colors are and how the model is structured
  • The four DISC colors (red, yellow, green, blue) explained in simple terms
  • A short DISC color test to discover your preferred color
  • Practical applications in teams, leadership, and recruitment & selection
  • Common misconceptions about DISC and how to use the model correctly

What is the DISC model, and how do DISC colors work?

The DISC model is based on the work of psychologist William Moulton Marston. He identified four behavioral tendencies:

  • Dominance
  • Influence
  • Steadiness
  • Conscientiousness.
In many practical situations, these behavioral styles are represented by DISC colors: red, yellow, green, and blue.

The test does not measure intelligence or talent. DISC looks at your preferred behavior: how you communicate, make decisions, respond to pressure, and collaborate with others. Everyone has all four colors within them, but usually one or two colors stand out the most.

The major advantage of working with DISC colors is their simplicity. Colors are easy to remember and serve as a neutral language for discussing behavior. Instead of saying, “You’re difficult,” you can say, “You’re exhibiting a lot of red behavior right now.” This makes conversations less personal and much more constructive.

Discover your DISC color profile

The four DISC colors explained

Keep in mind that every person possesses all the colors, but certain colors sometimes come to the fore more often.

Red: Dominant, direct, and results-oriented (D)

People with a lot of red in their DISC profile like pace, clear goals, and tangible results. You easily take the lead, speak your mind, and like it when things happen quickly.

In meetings, you get right to the point. You ask, “What are we going to do?” instead of “How does everyone feel about this?” You can be firm in your communication, especially when plans are delayed or others keep getting bogged down in details.

The strength of red is decisiveness, the ability to make decisions, and a focus on performance. The pitfall is that you can sometimes come across as overly direct or impatient. Consciously giving space to green and blue colleagues helps you make better decisions together.

Yellow: Influential, enthusiastic, and inspiring (I)

Yellow DISC colors represent energy, ideas, and connecting with people. You’re often optimistic, enjoy talking, and quickly spot opportunities. Presenting, networking, and getting others on board with a story come naturally to you.

In groups, you’re quick to speak up. You connect people, crack jokes, and enjoy thinking out loud. Rules and details can slow you down, especially if they interrupt your creative flow.

The strength of yellow is influence, inspiration, and creating momentum. The pitfall is that you sometimes fail to follow through on commitments or take on too much at once. Collaborating with blue and green colleagues helps ensure structure and continuity.

Green: Stable, loyal, and supportive (S)

People with a lot of green in their DISC profile value stability, collaboration, and mutual trust. You’re often calm, patient, and focused on creating a pleasant atmosphere.

You’re a good listener, help your colleagues, and believe it’s important for everyone to feel seen. When changes occur, you first consider the impact on people, not just goals and numbers.

The strength of green is loyalty, team spirit, and reliability. The pitfall is having difficulty saying “no” or avoiding confrontational conversations. You can learn from red colleagues to make decisions more quickly at times and set clear boundaries.

Blue: Conscientious, analytical, and precise (C)

Blue DISC colors represent quality, logic, and structure. You like to work meticulously, verify information, and want to understand exactly how things work.

You ask critical questions, pay attention to details, and dislike sloppiness. In conversations, you prefer to let facts speak rather than emotions. You want to think things through carefully before taking a position.

The strength of blue is reliability, clear analysis, and high-quality standards. The pitfall is that you may come across as slow or aloof, especially to red or yellow colleagues. Consciously explaining why you ask questions helps prevent misunderstandings.

Request your DISC color report

How does a DISC color test work?

A DISC test consists of statements or sets of words where you indicate what best and least suits you. Often, you describe how you see yourself in work situations. There are no right or wrong answers: it’s about your natural preferences.

Your answers are converted into scores on the four scales (D, I, S, and C). Those scores are then translated into your DISC color profile. Most people recognize themselves in a combination of two dominant colors.

A professional report not only shows which color(s) suit you, but also how you communicate, what you need from others, what causes you stress, and where your talents lie.

On this page, you can take a free, short color test.

DISC Colors in Teams and Collaboration

It’s interesting to know your DISC colors, but what matters most is what you actually do with that information.

Understanding Team Dynamics

In a team with a lot of red, the goals and results are usually clear-cut, but the atmosphere can be tense.

In a team with a lot of green, the atmosphere is often excellent, but difficult decisions are sometimes put off. By mapping out the DISC colors, you can see where tensions and opportunities lie.

A balanced team combines colors: red for direction, yellow for energy, green for support, and blue for quality. Discussing colors prevents differences from becoming personal.

Distributing Tasks Wisely Based on DISC Colors

For example, have red team members monitor deadlines and make decisions.

Yellow team members can give presentations, facilitate brainstorming sessions, or scout out new opportunities. Green team members excel at onboarding, coaching, and customer relations. Blue team members oversee scheduling, quality, and risks.

By assigning work based on DISC colors, you increase both engagement and results. People do what energizes them and what they’re good at.

Leadership and DISC Colors

Leaders often exhibit a mix of colors but usually have a preferred style.

Red leadership is direct and decisive; yellow leadership is inspiring and motivating; green leadership is coaching and caring; blue leadership is analytical and meticulous.

Effective leaders know their own profile and tailor their style to others.

For example, a green team member needs more time and support during change than a red team member. Using the language of DISC colors makes this concrete and open to discussion.

DISC Colors in Recruitment & Selection

In selection processes, a DISC color test helps to objectively assess behavior and potential. You can better determine whether someone is a good fit for the role, the team, and the manager’s leadership style.

It’s important, however, never to use DISC as the sole decision-making criterion.

Always combine insights from DISC colors with experience, competencies, references, and a thorough interview. This prevents color profiles from being used as a “label” rather than as a development tool.

Use DISC colors in your selection process

Common mistakes with DISC colors

1. “You’re red, so…” DISC describes preferred behavior, not character. People are more than just one color. It’s a tool for understanding behavior, not a fixed label.

2. Confusing color with competence Red behavior doesn’t automatically mean good leadership, and a lot of blue doesn’t guarantee flawless analysis. DISC colors indicate how someone approaches things, not whether they’re capable of performing at a high level.

3. Focusing on only one color Most profiles are a mix. For example, someone might be red-yellow (direct and inspiring) or green-blue (caring and precise). It’s precisely these combinations that make DISC rich and useful.

4. Using DISC as an excuse : “That’s just how I am; I’m Red.” That phrase may sound tempting at times, but it doesn’t do justice to personal development. Understanding DISC colors is actually meant to help you become more flexible, not to justify behavior.

Frequently Asked Questions About DISC Colors

Can my DISC colors change over time? Your core preference often remains fairly stable, but nuances can shift due to new roles, experiences, and conscious development. Under stress, you may also exhibit different behavior than in relaxed situations.

Is one DISC color better than another? No. Each color brings both strengths and pitfalls. Successful teams need a variety of DISC colors, precisely to complement one another. The question isn’t which color is “good,” but which color is appropriate in the context.

Can I get some use out of DISC colors on my own without an official report? Yes. Simply having a conversation using color-based language provides a lot of insight. The mini-test on this page will help you get started. For deeper insights, graphs, and concrete development advice, a full test is highly recommended.

Is DISC the same as other color models?

There are several models that use colors. The basis of DISC colors lies in Marston’s four-factor model (D, I, S, C). Other models sometimes use different names or additional dimensions. It’s important to use the same terminology within a single organization.

¿Qué es el desarrollo del liderazgo?

El desarrollo del liderazgo consiste en ampliar el repertorio de comportamientos de los directivos. ¿Cómo funciona el desarrollo del liderazgo mediante evaluaciones?

1. Identificar el comportamiento

Una evaluación de la personalidad muestra qué preferencias de comportamiento muestra una persona bajo presión, al trabajar en equipo o al dirigir a otros.

Los motivadores explican por qué una persona muestra un comportamiento determinado. Esto aclara la motivación, los factores que aportan energía y los que la consumen, así como el compromiso.

4. Vincular el desarrollo al perfil del puesto

Determina qué competencias son necesarias para el puesto: orientar, planificar, marcar el rumbo, analizar, delegar y colaborar.

5. Imponer la formación de forma específica

El término «CanMEDS» es muy habitual en el ámbito de la enfermería. También se habla de «funciones» o «competencias» CanMEDS. Los roles CanMEDS se utilizan principalmente en las profesiones paramédicas, pero hoy en día también se aplican al Registro de Enfermeros Especialistas, al Registro de Calidad de Cuidados y Asistencia y al Registro de Profesionales Sanitarios. Por supuesto, queda por aclarar qué son exactamente estos roles CanMEDS y cuál es su objetivo. [caption id="attachment_8414" align="aligncenter" width="300"] Fuente: Royal College of Canada[/caption]  

¿Qué son los roles CanMEDS?

Los roles CanMEDS han sido desarrollados por el Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada. El término en sí es una contracción de «Canadian Medical Education Directives for Specialists». El sistema CanMEDS se aplica a nivel internacional para definir las funciones de los distintos profesionales sanitarios. En general, se distingue entre siete funciones diferentes, cada una de las cuales tiene su propia competencia o aptitud.

El proveedor de formación acreditada distribuye los puntos entre un máximo de tres competencias CanMEDS. Como especialista en enfermería, debes indicar tú mismo la distribución de puntos al introducir una prueba o al registrar otras actividades de desarrollo profesional en el Registro de Especialistas en Enfermería. Los cuidadores, los expertos en garantía de calidad y los enfermeros no están obligados a hacerlo.

El desarrollo de las competencias CanMEDS: las 7 funciones

En cualquier caso, es importante saber sobre qué temas debes realizar este tipo de actividades para poder desarrollar determinadas competencias. Por ello, conviene ofrecer aquí un resumen de estas competencias y algunos ejemplos:
  1. Actuación profesional: ¿he adquirido conocimientos sobre el cuidado de clientes o pacientes?
Algunos ejemplos son la fisiología, la anatomía, las limitaciones y los cuadros clínicos, el diagnóstico, la farmacología, el autocontrol, el apoyo y el acompañamiento, la intervención, la prevención, la psicología y la psiquiatría, los medios de ayuda y apoyo, las técnicas de enfermería, el plan de cuidados, etc.
  1. Comunicación: ¿He adquirido conocimientos sobre la interacción con los usuarios o pacientes?
Algunos ejemplos son: técnicas de conversación, influencia en el comportamiento, empoderamiento, uso de las TIC, redes sociales, motivación, comunicación teórica, etc.
  1. Colaboración: ¿He adquirido conocimientos sobre la colaboración con el personal sanitario, así como con los pacientes y los usuarios y las instituciones sanitarias?
Algunos ejemplos son la elaboración de informes, la atención integrada, el traspaso de pacientes, la colaboración multidisciplinar, la dinámica de grupo, etc.
  1. Ciencia y conocimiento: ¿He aprendido más para poder reflexionar sobre mi profesionalidad y los motivos de mis acciones?
Algunos ejemplos son la aplicación de la ciencia, la práctica basada en la evidencia, la metodología de investigación, la retroalimentación, etc.
  1. Actuación socialmente responsable: ¿He aprendido más sobre los contextos sociales y las medidas de promoción de la salud?
Algunos ejemplos son la prevención, los contextos culturales, la educación sanitaria, la intervención proactiva, la promoción de un estilo de vida saludable, la epidemiología, etc.
  1. Organización: ¿He adquirido más conocimientos sobre cómo se puede organizar la atención sanitaria?
Algunos ejemplos son las formas de alojamiento a pequeña escala, la asequibilidad de la atención, la evaluación de necesidades, la atención a distancia, la seguridad de los pacientes, el ambiente de trabajo, la gestión organizativa, etc.
  1. Calidad y profesionalidad: ¿He aprendido más sobre los estándares profesionales y la garantía de calidad?
Algunos ejemplos son el código deontológico, los perfiles profesionales, las directrices y normas, las asociaciones profesionales y la imagen del sector, los registros y sistemas de calidad, la legislación y la normativa en materia de cuidados, etc.  

La importancia de las competencias CanMeds en enfermería

Hace falta decir que el sector sanitario es un sector de gran valor social, tanto para las instituciones sanitarias y los profesionales sanitarios como para los propios usuarios de los servicios sanitarios. El objetivo de las CanMeds es perfeccionar aún más las competencias que son de gran importancia para el desarrollo de un sector sanitario mejorado, de modo que la atención que se pueda prestar a quienes la necesitan sea de mejor calidad y más profesional. Además, las CanMEDS ofrecen una visión clara del estado actual de las competencias de los profesionales sanitarios, lo que permite introducir todas las mejoras necesarias.  

Competencias CanMEDS en su organización

Al utilizar un cuestionario CanMEDS de retroalimentación de 360 grados, sus empleados reciben una mejor retroalimentación, lo que les permite desarrollarse más rápidamente y aumentar la calidad de la atención sanitaria. Además, usted podrá evaluar mejor el desempeño de sus empleados.

CanMEDS en 2025. ¿Más relevantes que nunca?

En 2025, las competencias CanMEDS habrán adquirido una posición aún más destacada en el sector sanitario. Las siete funciones constituyen ahora la base de prácticamente todos los sistemas de calidad y itinerarios formativos, como la formación superior en enfermería (HBO V).

Debido a la creciente digitalización y personalización de la asistencia sanitaria, se han ampliado especialmente los roles de «Comunicación» y «Acción social». Los profesionales sanitarios deben dominar ahora tanto la comunicación física como la digital, alternando con frecuencia entre diferentes plataformas.

La integración de la inteligencia artificial en el diagnóstico y los planes de tratamiento ha transformado la competencia «Ciencia y conocimiento». El pensamiento crítico y la alfabetización digital se han convertido en elementos esenciales para utilizar eficazmente las herramientas tecnológicas sin perder la dimensión humana.

La experiencia de la pandemia ha dado lugar a una nueva valoración de las competencias de «Colaboración y organización». Los profesionales sanitarios colaboran ahora de forma mucho más flexible en equipos variables, tanto dentro como fuera del entorno sanitario tradicional.

El Registro de Calidad también se ha adaptado. Ahora se exigen requisitos más estrictos en cuanto a la distribución de los puntos de acreditación entre las distintas áreas de competencia, prestando especial atención a la integración de estas habilidades en la práctica diaria.

De este modo, las funciones de CanMEDS no solo han seguido siendo relevantes, sino que en 2025 han adquirido un papel aún más central.
